analytic.title: Implementation and Evaluation of Adaptive Cache Insertion Policies for Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Memory caches are a key source of unpredictability in today's cyber-physical systems. This fact is mainly due to the high time penalties caused by cache misses. A block that needs to be replaced may need up to 100 times more cycles than a block already in the cache (cache hit). Several studies in the area of realtime systems were carried out aiming to minimize the impact of cache memories on the Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) of real-time systems. The main approaches are related to cache line replacement policies and cache partitioning mechanisms, as the LRU-based adaptive insertion policies LIP, BIP and DIP, which were developed to try to mitigate the trashing problem of LRU. Several studies have already proven that replacement policies can be influenced by cache parameters, but none of them presented an analysis of the impact of these parameters on policies applied to cache partitions.

In this scenario, this work aims to provide an analysis of the impact that cache-related parameters have on the adaptive cache insertion policies applied to a set of benchmarks. For this, we used a cache profile simulator. The results obtained prove that parameters as cache partition size and the number of ways, in fact, play an important factor in the performance and schedulability of applications.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Under the impulsion of trends such as Internet-of-Things (IoT) and the Internet-of-Everything (IoE), the embedded systems have proliferated and seen adoption in diverse applications ranging from automotive, medical, and industrial automation. In these sectors, the advent of advanced algorithms and new paradigms such as AI controllers, combined with the introduction of high-bandwidth sensors have led System-on-Chip (SoC) designers to continuously integrate advanced computing techniques. Consequently, in some applications, it is common to find SoCs featuring multiple cores, specialized hardware accelerators, and even tightly integrated Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) [1].

While the aforementioned techniques are successful in reducing the overall average execution time, they all suffer from a common and well-known bottleneck: the shared memory sub-system [2]. In fact, the off-chip memory technology speed (e.g., DRAM) has always evolved at a slower pace than the speed of the on-chip logic [3]. Naturally, this observation has been exacerbated by the integration of multiple execution units within a single SoC architecture (MPSoC). Traditionally, this problem has been addressed by the integration of caches, lowlatency, and high-bandwidth small piece of on-chip memory.

However, the reduced capacity of the caches combined with the growing size of applications introduces another challenge: the online management of its content. This management has a huge influence on the eventual execution time of the system's tasks as accessing a piece of data present in the cache (i.e., a cache hit) is orders of magnitude faster than fetching data located in the off-chip memory (i.e., a cache miss). A sizeable amount of research has explored how tailoring the cache architecture can improve the predictability and execution time of Hard Real-Time (HRT) systems [2], including cache partitioning techniques [2], [4], cache-aware real-time schedulers [5], and analyses of the cache eviction policies [6].

In the context of HRT systems, designing and implementing a near-optimal cache eviction policy is essential, as the gains in execution time have a direct impact on the schedulability ratios and the utilization of the target platform. Standard and state-of-the-art cache architectures feature either the Least-Recently-Used policy (LRU), the Pseudo-Random-Eviction policy (RANDOM), or the First-in-First-out policy (FIFO) [6].

Considering the fact that LRU-based replacement policies are susceptible to thrashing when the required application data is greater than the available cache, in [7] the authors proposed simple changes to the insertion policy to reduce the number of cache misses for memory-intensive applications, named Adaptive Insertion Policies. The LRU Insertion Policy (LIP) that places the incoming line in the LRU position instead of the Most-Recently Used (MRU) position, Bimodal Insertion Policy (BIP) that modifies LIP by inserting occasionally (with a low probability) the incoming line in the MRU position, and Dynamic Insertion Policy (DIP) that chooses between LIP and BIP at run-time based on a counter of cache misses, have presented interesting results when compared to LRU [7], but their impact on the schedulability of real-time systems has not been studied yet. Moreover, the original DIP evaluation in [7] has not studied its behavior when varying the number of ways and the impact of the cache miss counter size.

In this paper, we extended the analysis of the adaptive insertion policies proposed in [7], considering the context of real-time systems. By implementing the adaptive insertion policies in a cache simulator (cachegrind [8]), we are able to evaluate the behavior of the policies when varying the cache parameters. Moreover, by applying the reduction on the number of cache misses of the DIP policy into the schedulability analysis, we can observe its impact on the schedulability ratio of real-time systems. In summary, the contributions of this article are the following:

• We extend the original DIP evaluation proposed in [7] by including experiments varying the number of ways and the cache miss counter (PSEL) size, as well as experiments varying the cache partition size and two benchmark suites.

Our new results demonstrate that DIP is sensitive to the number of ways and the PSEL counter size influences the execution of tasks and that a large size enables DIP to approximate the optimal choice of policy.
• We implement the adaptive insertion policies (LIP, BIP, and DIP) in an open-source cache simulator (cachegrind), which can enable comparison to other policies and new research on the subject.

• We apply the DIP reduction on the number of cache misses into the schedulability of real-time tasks, using a fixed-priority non-preemptive policy. The use of DIP can improve the schedulability ratio even by 50% when compared to LRU. This paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces all the ancillary notions regarding cache eviction policies and Adaptive Insertion Policies. In Section III, an overview of the cache-related research for Hard Real-Time Systems is offered. A bird-eye overview of the implementation and evaluation setup within the Cachegrind framework is provided in Section IV. Finally, a complete evaluation of the DIP eviction policy is provided and discussed in Section V.

div.head: II. BACKGROUND
div.p: Over the years, computing systems have become more efficient. In particular, processors have had a fast and impressive evolution. In contrast, the memories, despite the significant developments, did not keep pace with the processor [9]. This difference ended up impacting the performance of the computer, which, even having a high-speed processor, encountered significant delays in accessing and transferring data.

The demands on memory performance and capacity have increased as computer systems are applied to increasingly complex projects, giving rise to different memory specifications, with different construction technologies and consequently with increasing production costs [10].

The needs around memory bring complex challenges to the design of practical systems. If, on the one hand, larger and faster memory is desired, the cost of that memory must also be considered [11]. For this reason, the development of a memory hierarchy proved to be imperative, using more than one component or technology in order to satisfy the different performance needs that systems may have [3], [12].

The cache memory is one of the components of the memory hierarchy. It improves the average performance of computer system, because of its faster access, so the cache plays as an intermediary between the processor and the main memory, keeping data that have more probability to be used in a near future, according to temporal locality principle. Every time a cache is accessed, two events may occur, a cache hit, when this data is in the cache, or a cache miss, when the required data is not in the cache and must be brought from main memory.

When a cache miss occurs, the incoming line must be inserted at some position of cache, replacing an old line. To do it, cache uses a replacement policy to choose which of the presented line will be evicted and where the incoming line will be inserted. Some well-know replacement policies are RANDOM, FIFO, LRU and PSEUDO-LRU.

The RANDOM policy, as the name suggests, chooses the line to be replaced randomly. The FIFO (First In, First Out) algorithm considers the order of entry of a line into the cache. When all lines are full and a new one needs to be inserted, this policy takes the first line inserted among those present and replaces it with the new one.

The idea behind the LRU (Least Recently Used) policy is to order the lines according to how recently they have been accessed. Regardless of whether a memory access leads to a hit or a miss, the line is promoted to the MRU position and causes all other lines to move to the next position. During an eviction, the least recently used line is designated as the victim.

The PSEUDO-LRU algorithm, also known as tree-LRU, consists of saving the cache memory status in a binary tree. Each node in this tree is a bit, which can be interpreted as an arrow. When a cache hit occurs, the bits pointing to that memory location are inverted. When a cache miss occurs, the new data will replace the line pointed by the bits, which will then be inverted.

div.head: A. Adaptive Insertion Policies
div.p: In [7], three new replacement policies are introduced: LIP, BIP and DIP, also known as Adaptive Insertion Policies. LIP (LRU Insertion Policy) inserts the new line in the LRU position and promotes the lines from the LRU position to the MRU position only if they are accessed while in the LRU position.

BIP (Bimodal Insertion Parameter) is a variation of LIP. It uses a bimodal throttle parameter to define the position in which the incoming line will be inserted. The bimodal throttle parameter ranges from 0 to 1 and it can be seen as the probability of the incoming line to be inserted in the LRU position. Note that if the bimodal parameter is set to 1, the incoming line will be inserted in MRU position (i.e., BIP will behave like the LRU policy), but if the parameter is set to 0, the insertion will take place in the LRU position, so BIP will behave like the LIP policy.

The last policy proposed in [7] is DIP (Dynamic Insertion Policy), which aims to choose the best policy between LRU and BIP according to which incurs in fewer misses based on a cache miss counter (named PSEL) that is incremented or decremented at run-time. These adaptive insertion policies were compared against LRU in terms of cache misses and presented better performance. However, the insertion policies were not evaluated considering the schedulability of real-time systems, which we believe could present interesting results. Moreover, the evaluation of the DIP policy is limited, since it did not vary the number of ways in the cache nor the size of the PSEL counter. In this work, we aim at extending the evaluation of the adaptive insertion policies, especially for the DIP policy, and assess the benefits of using DIP in real-time systems through a schedulability ratio evaluation.

div.head: III. RELATED WORK
div.p: As noted earlier, such cache line replacement policies are the features that most influence cache memory predictability. The authors in [6] present a quantitative analysis of the impact of FIFO, LRU, MRU, and PLRU eviction policies on the predictability of systems, through the analysis of how quickly knowledge about cache hits and misses is selected. The results of this analysis demonstrate that no policy performs better than LRU for high-location workloads. LRU is the most used policy; however, it has disadvantages for memory-intensive workloads. Several authors propose solutions to this problem. Qureshi et al. [7] proposed three adaptive insertion policies based on the LRU search (as described in Section II-A).

Other adaptations of the LRU policy aiming to increase the predictability of real-time systems are presented in the works of [13]- [17]. In [13], the authors discuss the deficiency of existing cache line replacement policies in using memory level parallelism to optimize performance in long-latency memory access and propose a new policy capable of analyzing the different costs that cache misses may have when being served individually or in parallel, named MLP-aware. It is also proposed a mechanism capable of dynamically choosing between the MLP-aware policy and a traditional cache line replacement policy according to its effectiveness in reducing the number of memory-related interrupts. During tests and evaluations, the presented MLP-aware policy demonstrated 23% better performance than traditional LRU [13].

The PRETI [14] cache scheme is a small modification made to shared caches that use LRU policy to cater for multitasking processors and that ensures scalability of real-time tasks by allowing these tasks to obtain private cache space during its execution. As a result, PRETI allows WCET analysis to produce more accurate estimates.

In [16], is proposed a cache line replacement policy capable of reducing the number of cache misses in preemptive scenarios while maintaining traditional LRU performance in non-preemptive scenarios, resulting in improved performance and predictability in multitasking systems. DM-LRU [17] is a cache partitioning-aware policy based on a memory abstraction called Deterministic Memory (DM) [18]. DM-LRU classifies the program address space in two distinct memory categories according to the importance of predictability or average performance. The results showed that this approach can provide lower tasks WCETs with less overhead and programming complexity compared to the standard LRU and cache-blocking-based approaches.

Qureshi, Suleman and Patt [15] targeted the problem from the waste of addresses in the memory cache when the programs do not have spatial locality. Caches are designed to work with a block size that aims to explore spatial locality. However, when programs do not have this property, the cache area is wasted, as the block size cache stores several unused lines. Line Distillation (LDIS) holds in the cache only the lines that are referenced and evicts lines that are not referenced while loading the cache. Rather than ejecting an entire block containing multiple rows, this technique provides more granularity in managing the cache area.

div.head: IV. IMPLEMENTATION
div.p: This Section discusses the implementation of the Adaptive Insertion Policies in the cachegrind simulator [8]. It introduces and overviews cachegrind in Section IV-A and presents the implementation in Section IV-B.

div.head: A. General Structure in Cachegrind
div.p: Cachegrind is an open-source tool and one of the standard features provided by Valgrind (an instrumentation framework for building dynamic analysis tools) [8]. It simulates and generates detailed profiles of the whole cache hierarchy.

Cachegrind requires as input the cache partition size, the number of ways, the line size and the replacement policy to be used and provides information about the number of instructions executed, number of data references, number of access and misses to the first level of the instruction and data cache, number of reference data, and number of misses of the LLC.

Within cachegrind code, whenever there is an instruction or data reference, it simulates the cache access using either a Ior D-cache, as shown in Fig. 1. The target cache is passed as a parameter (&L1 or &D1 in the call to the is_miss), together with the address' set and tag. Within is_miss, the appropriate cache eviction policy is applied through a function pointer to the function which implements the eviction policy algorithm. We modified this part of the cachegrind by adding functions for each adaptive insertion policy (LIP, BIP, and DIP). If there is a miss in the first level of the cache, then cachegrind calls again is_miss passing the LLC as parameter.

div.head: B. Implementation in Cachegrind
div.p: For LIP, the implementation follows the one in Listing 1. set no represents the number of sets and c → assoc the cache associativity. First, the required tag is retrieved (line 3) and if this tag is found in the cache, that tag is promoted to MRU position (set [1]), shuffling the rest down (line 7). However, when a cache miss occurs, i.e., the required tag is not in the cache, it is inserted into the LRU position (line 9). BIP behaves as LRU or LIP for any cache hit (i.e., promoting recently accessed line to MRU position), but for a cache miss, the bimodal throttle parameter is necessary to decide how the policy will behave. The bimodal throttle parameter and a randomly generated number (prob) are used to define the behavior of BIP, as shown in line 7 of Listing 2. If prob is greater or equal to the bimodal throttle parameter times 100, BIP acts like LIP (line 9), otherwise, it acts like LRU (line 11). Note that if the bimodal throttle parameter is 1, BIP behaves always like LRU, and if it is 0, BIP behaves always like LIP. DIP was implemented using the global mechanism shown in Fig. 2. The global mechanism uses two auxiliary directories with copies of blocks from the main cache. In each directory, the LRU (ATD-LRU directory) and BIP (ATD-BIP directory) policies are applied exclusively. The policy used in the main cache is the one that counts the least number of cache misses in their respective directories. For this, a binary counter, named PSEL, is incremented at every miss that occurs in the directory under the BIP policy and is decremented whenever an miss occurs in the directory under the LRU policy. If the most significant bit of PSEL is 0, LRU policy is used, otherwise BIP policy is used in the main cache (MTD). Listing 3 shows the DIP code implemented in cachegrind. Two copies of the cache were created (lines 2 and 3) and initialized during the cachegrind startup. One of the versions is used by the BIP policy (cache_bip -line 11), while the other one is used by the LRU policy (cache_lru -line 12). The PSEL counter was implemented with 4, 8, 10, 11, 20 and 40 bits and it could be decremented to 0 (line 18) and incremented to its maximum value in binary (PSEL max -line 15). We always initialize the PSEL counter halfway through its range (PSEL msb) for fairness, so any miss can lead to BIP or LRU policy. At the end, if PSEL is greater than or equal to PSEL msb (line 20), the chosen policy would be BIP (line 23), otherwise, it would be LRU (line 21). For example, for a 4-bit PSEL, its range is from 0 to 15 corresponding to the values 0b0000 and 0b1111 in binary, respectively. The value of PSEL msb is set to 8, which corresponds to 1000, that is, the first value to have 1 in the most significant bit, which is also the value at which PSEL was initialized, as it is in the middle of the range [0, 15].

Listing 3: DIP implementation in cachegrind. 1 i n i t i a l i z e c a c h e m a i n ; / * i n i t i a l i z e MTD * / 2 i n i t i a l i z e c a c h e l r u ; / * i n i t i a l i z e ATD-LRU * / 3 i n i t i a l i z e c a c h e b i p ; / * I n i t i a l i z e ATD-BIP * / The overarching objective of this section is to assess and understand the run-time behavior of the adaptive insertion policies (in special DIP due to its better performance) and their applicability to real-time systems. To this end, we have used the extended version of Cachegrind [8] described in Section IV, which, as a reminder, features the Adaptive Insertion Policies as well as a conventional eviction policy (e.g., LRU).

Except for results in Section V-E, all the experiments presented in our evaluations have used a selected set of the benchmark applications issued from the Mibench [19] and Cortex [20] benchmark suites. The selection of the benchmarks has been done with the purpose of creating a heterogeneous benchmark set composed of memory-intensive and low-memory demand applications. Memory intensive applications are issued from the Cortex suite and include Kmeans, svd3, spc, and pca. Whereas, low-memory demand applications are issued from the Mibench suite and include basicmath, bitcount, qsort, susan, jpeg, stringsearch, dijkstra, bf, sha, gsm, fft, adpcm, and crc32.
Throughout the evaluation, the aforementioned benchmarks have been executed for a wide range of cache configurations. More accurately, three factors have been taken into account:

(1) the total cache size (ranging from 1 KB to 2 MB); (2) the number of ways (e.g., 2, 4, 8, and 16); and (3) the cache replacement policy (LRU, BIP, and DIP). Additionally, in the case of DIP, the size of PSEL is also subject to variations. However, the cache line size is fixed to 64 bytes for all the experiments. The BIP throttle parameter was set to 1/64 as also used in [7]. Finally, note that for space and clarity reasons, only an interesting set of all the results obtained are presented 1 .

The rest of this section is organized as follows. Section V-A shows the LIP, BIP, and DIP performances in terms of cache misses and compares them against LRU. Section V-B explores the impact of the PSEL size in the DIP policy, while Section V-C assesses the relationship between the number of ways and DIP performance. Section V-D shows the PSEL evolution at run-time for a selected set of benchmarks. Finally, Section V-E shows the impact of using DIP on the schedulability ratios through the generation of synthetic task sets.

div.head: A. Cache Miss Evaluation
div.p: In this experiment, we evaluate BIP and DIP and compare them to LRU with respect to the amount of cache misses each benchmark experiences for the previously mentioned policies. The results for kmeans-small, pca-small, and svd3-small are displayed in Fig. 3. Each of these benchmarks is simulated on a platform assuming an 8 way-associative cache with a total size varying from 1 KB to 2 MB (x-axis) and for different eviction policies (bar clusters). Following the setup in [7], the PSEL counter has a size of 10 bits and is initially set to 512, half of the highest number (i.e., 1024). The amount of cache misses for each cache configuration (i.e., size and policy) is reported on the y-axis and is normalized w.r.t. the baseline (i.e., the same cache size with LRU). each bar cluster, a smaller bar than LRU implies that the policy has fewer cache misses and, thus, a reduced execution time.

A first observation from the results displayed in Fig. 3 is that BIP and DIP are not always better than LRU. In each of the benchmarks displayed in Fig. 3, we observe a range of cache sizes for which the amount of cache misses is smaller than LRU. These ranges vary from one benchmark to another, meaning that the efficiency of the Adaptive Insertion Policies depends on the amount of data needed by the benchmark and the cache size. For instance, as illustrated by Fig. 3a, kmeans-small experiences fewer cache misses using BIP and DIP when the cache size is 2048 KB and 4096 KB. Similarly, pca-small and svd3-small experience fewer cache misses for cache sizes ranging from 16 KB to 512 KB and 2 KB to 8 KB, respectively. The second observation is that, unlike BIP, the DIP policy always tends to replicate the performance of the best policy for a given cache size.

div.head: B. PSEL Size Analysis
div.p: In [7], the original paper introducing the DIP policy, the size of the PSEL counter is arbitrarily set to 10 bits. However, its size (and subsequently its resolution) can potentially influence the policy switching decision. The objective of this set of experiments is to evaluate the impact of the PSEL size on the amount of cache misses occurring during the execution of pca-small and svd3-small benchmarks.

For this experiment (see Fig. 4), we assume a 128 KB large 8-way associative cache and run the benchmarks using the LRU, BIP and DIP policies (bar clusters). We vary the size of PSEL (expressed in bits) on the x-axis and report the amount of cache misses occurring on the y-axis. Each bar is normalized over the cache misses occurring using LRU.

From Fig. 4, one can clearly see that the actual size of the PSEL counter does not seem to have any impact on the cache misses of svd3-small. On the other hand, pca-small is slightly affected by the PSEL counter size. As shown in Fig. 4a, for small PSEL sizes (i.e., from 2 bits to 10 bits included), DIP incurs more cache misses than the BIP policy. However, as the PSEL counter size increases, the gap between DIP and BIP fades away. One can conclude that the PSEL counter size influences the execution of tasks and that a large size enables DIP to approximate the optimal choice of policy.

div.head: C. Associativity Influence on Cache Misses
div.p: In this experiment, we are interested in understanding the relationship between the associativity of the cache, the eviction policy and the amount of cache misses that a given benchmark will experience. As in the previous experiments, pca-small and svd3-small have been selected.

The cache architecture assumed has a constant total size of 128 KB, but a varying amount of ways (i.e., the amount of sets change for each configuration tested) and, in the case of DIP being the eviction policy, the PSEL register size is set to 10 bits as in [7].

The results are displayed in Fig. 5. The aforementioned benchmarks are run with different policies (bar cluster) and different number of ways (x-axis) ranging from 2 to 64. The amount of cache misses is reported on the y-axis and the height of each bar in a bar cluster is normalized over the LRU policy applied on the same cache configuration.

The selected benchmarks, pca-small (Fig. 5a) and svd3 (Fig. 5b) both highlight a different behavior. In the case of the former, one can observe that the amount of cache misses decreases linearly as the associativity increases until reaching a plateau at 16 ways. The good performance of BIP can be linked to an extremely sequential workload with low data re-utilization. On the other hand, for svd3-small the BIP policy fails to outperform LRU, hinting at a workload with higher data re-utilization. Globally, note that DIP is successful in always closely following the best-performing policy.

div.head: D. PSEL Behavior During the Benchmark Executions
div.p: The objective of this experiment is to understand the evolution of the PSEL counter during the execution of selected benchmarks. To this end, we instrumented our extended version of Cachegrind to collect and log the PSEL counter content. The traces for benchmarks basicmath-small, kmeans-small, and pca-small are displayed in Fig. 6.

In this set of experiments, we assume a 128 KB large 8-way associative cache having DIP for eviction policy and featuring a 10 bits wide PSEL register. Following the original paper [7], the PSEL counter is initialized with the value of 512, meaning that LRU is initially the policy selected. This frontier value separating BIP and LRU policies is drawn in red in Fig. 6.

In the case of basicmath and kmeans benchmarks (Fig.s 6a and 6b, respectively), the DIP policy continuously selects LRU as the policy in action. Throughout the execution of the two bechmarks, the PSEL value close to frontier value (i.e., 512), meaning that LRU incurs fewer caches misses than BIP. As can be observed in Fig. 6b, the last segment of the kmeans-small benchmark strongly prefers the LRU policy. Regarding the pca benchmark, one can clearly see that evolution of the PSEL value throughout the execution is segmented in two distinct areas. According to the PSEL value, before the 8000th instruction, the LRU policy is applied. Thereafter, the BIP policy is applied, meaning that this policy is the most adapted to this section of the program. Finally, one can note two pits on the right section of the plot (from the 11.000th to the 13.000th instructions and around the 15.000th instruction). These pits represent subsegments of the execution where using the LRU policy would bring a small advantage.

div.head: E. Schedulability Impact Evaluation
div.p: We compare the schedulability ratios for the synthetically generated periodic task sets with LRU, BIP and DIP under fixed-priority non-preemptive policy on a single core.

We generate a task set for each replacement policy. The task sets for BIP and DIP are obtained from the LRU task set by scaling the tasks' WCETs by the scaling factors from pca-small (128 KB cache) and svd3-small (1 KB cache) benchmarks. Each task set contains 8 tasks. We vary the utilization U from 0 to 1 with a step of 0.01 and generate 10000 triplets of task sets for each utilization. We apply the Emberson et al. unbiased method [21] to generate uniformly distributed random task-utilization values that sum to the total utilization U . For each task-utilization u i we randomly generate a period value t i in the range [10000, 1000000] microseconds with log uniform distribution and obtain the task's WCET as c i = u i ⋅ t i . Tasks have implicit deadlines and are assigned priorities based on the Rate-Monotonic policy [22] (i.e., the tasks with shorter periods have higher priorities). The scaling factors are obtained as the ratio between the WCETs under a given cache replacement policy and the standard LRU. We estimate the WCET for each policy based on the cachegrind task profile. We assume the same processor parameters as defined in [7]: 4 instructions per cycle, 6 cycles for a cache hit, and 270 cycles for a cache miss. Then, we apply the following equation to compute the WCET for each task:
div.formula: W CET = (I × CP I)+ (D M ISSES × M ISS P EN ALT Y )+ ((D REF S -D M ISSES) × HIT P EN ALT Y ) (1)
div.p: where I is the number of instructions, D MISSES is the number of cache misses, and D REFS the number of data references (all from the cachegrind output), CPI is the cycles per instruction (4), MISS PENALTY is the cache miss penalty (270), and HIT PENALTY the cache hit penalty (6) in processor cycles. The scaling factors under BIP and DIP are respectively 0.63149 and 0.65332 for pca-small and 1.07372 and 1.00018 for svd3-small. Fig. 7 shows the schedulability ratios (i.e., the number of schedulable task sets over all 10000 task sets that were generated) for fixed-priority non-preemptive [23] on a single core. In particular, Fig. 7a shows the schedulability ratio where the scaling factors of all tasks are based on pca-small, and Fig. 7b on svd3-small benchmark. The former favors BIP and the latter LRU. The results for pca-small show significant improvement of BIP over LRU reaching over 50% for high utilization rates. For svd3-small, LRU only slightly outperforms BIP. Most importantly, in both cases, DIP always follows the best policy incurring very little overhead.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this work, we perform an evaluation of the LRU-based Adaptive Insertion Policies LIP, BIP and DIP. For this end, we observe the impact of the cache geometry (i.e., total size and associativity) for each policy compared to LRU and we investigate the impact of the counter selector (PSEL) in DIP. The obtained results from a simulation environment (i.e., cachegrind) have shown that the cache size and the associativity play an important role in the performance of the Adaptive Insertion policies, while the variation of PSEL size are not that important. We also presented a schedulability evaluation for LRU, BIP and DIP using fixed-priority non-preemptive scheduling algorithm.

As future work we plan to implement and evaluate DIP in an open processor architecture such as RISC-V and explore the choice of cache related parameters to improve the replacement policies aiming HRT applications.
